findings.source_quote: αὕτη γὰρ ἡ ἐπιθυμία ἡ πονηρὰ τοῦ διαβόλου θυγάτηρ ἐστίν.
findings.english_quote: Working daughter of the devil is present in Lake (1907) Plate VIII and Palatina printed 125. Vulgata printed 64 instead says from the devil. These are different versional forms, not three identical Greek witnesses.
findings.issue: The selected Greek supports “the devil’s daughter,” but the note presents specific external attestations and their locations as established facts without supplying extracts or identifying them as unverified editorial reports. The supplied material does not establish those external readings. This is a provenance-disclosure defect, not evidence that the reported alternatives are false.
findings.suggested_revision: Retain “the devil’s daughter.” Supply bounded source extracts and provenance supporting the external attestations, or explicitly attribute them to an editorial report and disclose that their wording and locations are not verified by the material supplied for this review. Any replacement note requires fresh review.

findings.source_quote: Πάντων προέχουσα ἐπιθυμία γυναικὸς ἀλλοτρίας ἢ ἀνδρός
findings.english_quote: Another’s wife or husband preserves both sexes and the shared other-person construction. The Greek does not restrict this clause to a man desiring a wife.
findings.issue: This note is classified as “textual_variant,” although it explains the selected wording rather than identifying a different source reading. Notes c and d have the same classification problem: c supplies English interpretive alternatives, and d explains the preserved Lord/God distinction. This misrepresents translation explanations as textual-variant evidence.
findings.suggested_revision: Classify notes a, c, and d as translation, lexical, or source-wording explanations using the supported schema. Reserve “textual_variant” for a genuinely different reported source reading. Their explanatory wording need not be replaced merely to correct the classification.

findings.source_quote: αὕτη γὰρ ἡ ἐπιθυμία ἡ πονηρὰ τοῦ διαβόλου θυγάτηρ ἐστίν.
findings.english_quote: Working daughter of the devil is present in Lake (1907) Plate VIII and Palatina printed 125. Vulgata printed 64 instead says from the devil. These are different versional forms, not three identical Greek witnesses.
findings.issue: The simplified main text faithfully follows the selected daughter reading, but its shared note independently repeats unsupported, unqualified external-attestation claims. No supplied external extract establishes the named readings or locations. The alternatives can be disclosed without presenting their verification as settled.
findings.suggested_revision: Keep the selected main-text reading. Provide supporting extracts and provenance, or identify the external attestations as editorial reports whose wording and locations are not verified by the supplied review material. Review the revised note afresh.

findings.source_quote: Πάντων προέχουσα ἐπιθυμία γυναικὸς ἀλλοτρίας ἢ ἀνδρός
findings.english_quote: Another’s wife or husband preserves both sexes and the shared other-person construction. The Greek does not restrict this clause to a man desiring a wife.
findings.issue: The “textual_variant” classification does not match this note’s content: it explains the working reading, not a variant. The simplified edition likewise misclassifies note c’s English rendering alternatives and note d’s explanation of the selected divine titles as textual variants.
findings.suggested_revision: Reclassify notes a, c, and d as translation or source-wording explanations under the supported schema. Do not imply that their explanations constitute separately attested source readings.

summary: Both main texts were independently checked against all five paragraphs of the selected Greek; no concrete main-text fidelity defect was identified. Both preserve the death assertions, necessity, conditions, negations, divine titles, and servant/serve terminology. The contest/victory wording around crowning is contextual English expansion, not separately preserved Greek wording, but does not introduce a materially different assertion here. Both editions require corrections to note provenance and classification. This review does not verify external editions, manuscript images, or exhaustive collation, and it does not warrant replacing the disclosed working reading.
